drapeaux.note: Langue d'origine : anglais ; auteur : Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (article « Whorfianism », 2024). Retraduit depuis le français : « n'a pas tenté d'énoncer l'hypothèse ».

accroche: It bears the names of two linguists who never formulated it together, and never even called it that in their lifetimes.
contenu_vulgarise:
The film *Arrival* (2016) and hundreds of popular articles present it as established fact: the language you speak determines how you think, to the point that speakers of different languages would perceive the world differently. It's called “the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis.” Neither Edward Sapir nor Benjamin Lee Whorf ever formulated such a hypothesis, and they never did so together.

## A Hypothesis Nobody Stated

Sapir, a linguist and anthropologist trained by Franz Boas, died in 1939. Whorf, his student, a chemist by training turned passionate amateur linguist, died in 1941. Neither coauthored a text with the other, or published a formal, testable statement linking their two names. It was the anthropologist Harry Hoijer who, in 1953, at a Chicago conference devoted to Whorf's legacy, titled his paper “The Sapir-Whorf Hypothesis,” published the following year in the conference proceedings, *Language in Culture*. The name, and the joint attribution, were thus born after both men's deaths, from the pen of a third person who, according to later commentators, did not himself manage to state clearly the hypothesis he was christening.

Whorf wrote mostly popularizing essays, some of which suggest a strong version: language would shape thought to the point of becoming an almost insurmountable constraint. This is the reading that would inspire the famous example of the many Inuit words for snow. This strong version, often called linguistic determinism, is now rejected by nearly all linguists. Nothing prevents a speaker from perceiving or conceiving what their language doesn't name directly; otherwise translation or learning a foreign language would be impossible.

## What Controlled Experiments Show

A far more modest version has survived testing: language can influence, in certain specific tasks, the speed or manner in which information is processed, without ever preventing a person from perceiving it. The best-documented example involves colors. Russian has two basic words for what English puts under a single term, *blue*: *goluboy*, light blue, and *siniy*, dark blue. In 2007, in a study published in the *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences*, the psychologist Jonathan Winawer and his colleagues showed that Russian speakers tell two shades of blue apart faster when they fall into those two categories than when they belong to the same category. The advantage disappears if their verbal attention is occupied during the test, but not if their spatial attention is. The effect is thus carried by language, measurable but tiny and reversible: nothing like a perceptual prison.

## What It Shifts

The episode shifts things twice. First on substance: the idea that language imprisons thought, seductive and cinematic, gives way to a much narrower and verifiable version, a slight cognitive nudge, not a ceiling. Then on method: the name of a hypothesis can outlive, by decades, the absence of the hypothesis itself, carried by successive readings rather than by the original text. Checking what a text actually says remains, here as elsewhere, more instructive than checking what people repeat that it says.

repere.texte: The term “Sapir-Whorf hypothesis” appears only in 1954, coined by the anthropologist Harry Hoijer, 13 years after Whorf's death and 15 after Sapir's. According to the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Hoijer himself “did not attempt to state the hypothesis” he was naming.

carte.punch: The Sapir-Whorf hypothesis bears the names of two linguists who never formulated it together.
carte.idee: Sapir died in 1939, Whorf in 1941, without having written the hypothesis that bears their names. Harry Hoijer coined the name in 1954, after their deaths. The strong version, that language imprisons thought, is rejected; only a modest version survives, measured on specific tasks such as color.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: An update on what current research keeps and sets aside from the hypothesis popularized by the film.

quiz.question: What remains today of “the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis,” according to experimental data?
choix: Language completely determines what a speaker is able to perceive or conceive
Language can influence the speed or manner of processing information in specific tasks, without preventing a person from perceiving it
Sapir and Whorf demonstrated together, in a 1940 article, that Hopi grammar made linear time unthinkable
The most recent studies have entirely invalidated any effect of language on cognition
quiz.explication: Winawer and his colleagues (2007) show that Russian speakers, whose language has two basic words for light blue and dark blue, discriminate two shades on either side of that boundary faster, an effect that is measurable but reversible as soon as their verbal attention is occupied. Sapir and Whorf never published together, and both the strong deterministic version and its total rejection are caricatures of what the data actually show.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who coined the name Sapir-Whorf hypothesis, and when?
choix: The anthropologist Harry Hoijer, in 1954, after the deaths of both men
Edward Sapir himself, in an article published in 1938
Benjamin Lee Whorf, in a popularizing essay published in 1940
The linguist Noam Chomsky, in a critical article from the 1960s
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It was Harry Hoijer who, in 1954, 13 years after Whorf's death and 15 after Sapir's, gave the hypothesis its name, in a paper drawn from a 1953 Chicago conference.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In the study by Winawer and his colleagues (2007), what makes the Russian speakers' advantage in telling two shades of blue apart disappear?
choix: Occupying their verbal attention during the test
Occupying their spatial attention during the test
Asking them to close their eyes between two shades
Presenting the colors to them in random order
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Russian speakers' advantage disappears when their verbal attention is occupied during the test, but not when their spatial attention is, which shows that the effect does run through language.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What training had Benjamin Lee Whorf received before becoming a linguist?
choix: He was a chemical engineer, a graduate of MIT
He was an anthropologist, trained by Franz Boas at Columbia
He was a mathematician, specializing in formal logic
He was a philologist, a specialist in Native American languages
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Whorf graduated in chemical engineering from MIT in 1918 and became an amateur linguist only later, unlike Sapir, who had been trained by Boas.
